course.title: Cybercrime Investigation
course.description: A practical, evidence-centered course covering cybercrime investigation from case intake and lawful scope through preservation, acquisition concepts, endpoint and application evidence, network and log analysis, mobile and cloud evidence, timeline correlation, hypothesis testing, attribution discipline, and professional reporting. The course uses controlled synthetic or examiner-created data and emphasizes integrity, provenance, chain of custody, uncertainty, and defensible conclusions.
prerequisites: Basic networking concepts including IP, DNS, TCP/UDP, and logs
Basic Python is recommended for automation labs
Awareness that real evidence collection requires appropriate legal and organizational authority
learningOutcomes: Explain the evidence-centered workflow of a cybercrime investigation.
Plan preservation and acquisition activities with scope, authority, provenance, and chain-of-custody controls.
Calculate and verify SHA-256 hashes for supplied or examiner-created evidence copies.
Interpret endpoint, application, network, mobile, cloud, and online evidence with appropriate limitations.
Normalize heterogeneous event records into traceable timelines.
Correlate independent evidence sources and test competing hypotheses.
Recognize attribution limitations and possible anti-forensics indicators.
Produce professional findings and reports that distinguish observations, inferences, and limitations.
Complete an end-to-end synthetic cybercrime investigation and produce a structured case report.

modules.title: Foundations and Case Management
modules.description: Build the investigative mindset, terminology, scope discipline, and case-planning skills required before technical examination.

lessons.title: Cybercrime Investigation Fundamentals
lessons.description: Establish the investigative scope, evidence mindset, and distinction between cybercrime investigation, incident response, and digital forensic examination.
learningObjectives: define cybercrime investigation in evidence-centered terms
distinguish operational response from forensic examination
identify evidence sources relevant to an investigative question

notes.text: A cybercrime investigation seeks to establish facts about an event, systems, accounts, actions, timing, relationships, and impact using lawful and documented methods. Digital forensics supplies disciplined examination methods; incident response supplies operational context.

items: Evidence is useful only in relation to an investigative question and source context.
A technically interesting artifact is not automatically probative.
Observations, interpretations, and conclusions should be kept distinct.

notes.text: This course is educational and does not replace legal authority, organizational policy, or jurisdiction-specific advice.

practicals.title: Evidence-source map
practicals.description: Map a synthetic account-compromise allegation to evidence sources.
steps: List endpoint, identity, network, cloud, mobile, and online sources.
For each source state the fact it may support and one limitation.
practicals.solution: Use a table with source, artifact, question, volatility, and limitation.
practicals.output: Expected result: a scoped evidence map connecting sources to investigative questions.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes digital forensics in a cybercrime investigation?
options: It provides disciplined methods for preserving and examining digital evidence.
It is only used after prosecution.
quiz.answer: It provides disciplined methods for preserving and examining digital evidence.
quiz.explanation: Forensic methods contribute evidence handling and examination; they do not establish legal authority or automatically prove attribution.

summary: Investigation starts with questions, scope, authority, and evidence preservation.
Forensics is one part of the broader investigative process.

lessons.title: Case Intake, Scope, and Investigative Questions
lessons.description: Turn an allegation into a structured case plan with scope boundaries, assumptions, and evidence priorities.

items: Record the allegation and affected assets.
Confirm authority and scope.
Define questions the evidence must answer.
Prioritize preservation.
Record assumptions and open questions.
Set reporting milestones.
Scope prevents investigative drift.
An assumption is not an established fact.
Preservation priorities depend on volatility, relevance, and risk of loss.

quiz.question: Why record assumptions separately from facts?
options: To expose hypotheses that can be tested or revised.
quiz.answer: To expose hypotheses that can be tested or revised.
quiz.explanation: Visible assumptions make reasoning auditable and prevent hypotheses from silently becoming facts.

summary: A good case plan is question-driven.
Explicit scope and assumptions improve reviewability.

tasks.title: Create a defensible cybercrime case plan
tasks.problemStatement: Create a case plan identifying questions, evidence targets, preservation priorities, assumptions, limitations, and reporting milestones.
tasks.hint: Map each question to at least one evidence source and state what would weaken the hypothesis.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The plan is intentionally evidence-centered and records limitations rather than assuming attribution.

modules.title: Digital Evidence and Integrity
modules.description: Teach evidence characteristics, integrity controls, chain of custody, and documentation.

lessons.title: Digital Evidence Characteristics
lessons.description: Understand integrity, provenance, relevance, reliability, volatility, and the major locations where digital evidence can exist.
learningObjectives: explain why digital evidence is fragile and contextual
classify evidence by source and volatility
distinguish integrity from authenticity and attribution

notes.text: Digital evidence may be stored on computers, servers, mobile devices, network infrastructure, cloud services, or online platforms. Its meaning depends on source, acquisition method, system state, timestamps, and corroboration.

items: Live collection can change system state.
Preservation includes data and the documentation describing its handling.
A working copy can be examined while a preserved source remains protected.

practicals.title: Evidence classification
practicals.description: Classify synthetic artifacts by source and handling concern.
steps: Assign endpoint, network, mobile, cloud, or online category.
practicals.solution: Use a classification table rather than real data.
practicals.output: Expected result: a justified evidence-source matrix.

quiz.question: What is a defensible role for a hash?
options: It proves who created a file.
It detects changes to compared bytes.
quiz.answer: It detects changes to compared bytes.
quiz.explanation: Cryptographic hashes support integrity checking; they do not establish authorship or legal conclusions.

summary: Evidence must be evaluated with provenance and context.
Integrity, authenticity, relevance, and attribution are different concepts.

lessons.title: Chain of Custody and Evidence Documentation
lessons.description: Create traceable custody records and understand how documentation supports defensibility.

items: Use a unique evidence identifier.
Record date/time, handler, transfer, storage, and access information.
Record acquisition method and hashes when applicable.
Document the evidence state and relevant examiner actions.

notes.text: A cryptographic hash provides a compact integrity check. A matching digest supports byte-level consistency but does not by itself establish the provenance, meaning, or authorship of the data.

practicals.title: Hash a synthetic evidence file
practicals.description: Calculate and record SHA-256 for a harmless lab file.
steps: Create a small text evidence file.
Record evidence ID, size, SHA-256, and receipt time.
Copy the file and verify the digest.
Use the supplied Python script and a lab-created file only.
practicals.output: Expected result: a repeatable SHA-256 value and a documented verification event.

quiz.question: What does a matching SHA-256 digest primarily support?
quiz.explanation: Hash verification is an integrity control, not an attribution or legal test.

summary: Chain of custody records possession and handling.
Hashes help demonstrate integrity of compared data.

tasks.title: Build an evidence ledger
tasks.description: Create a machine-readable evidence ledger for synthetic evidence.
tasks.problemStatement: Validate evidence IDs, timestamps, required metadata, and SHA-256 format.
tasks.hint: Validate structure and hash format without inferring legal admissibility.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The validator tests structural properties only; it deliberately avoids legal or attribution conclusions.

modules.title: Preservation and Acquisition
modules.description: Develop first-response, preservation, acquisition planning, and working-copy discipline.

lessons.title: First Response and Crime Scene Preservation
lessons.description: Plan a safe, minimally disruptive response to a digital crime scene.

items: Ensure safety.
Establish authority and roles.
Control unnecessary access.
Document physical and device state.
Identify potentially volatile evidence.
Hand off to trained forensic personnel under procedure.

notes.text: Do not improvise live-system collection on real devices. Interaction can change evidence and should be performed only under approved procedures.

practicals.title: Synthetic scene record
practicals.description: Create a scene record from a written scenario.
steps: List actions that should be deferred.
practicals.output: Expected result: a complete scene record and forensic handoff note.

quiz.question: What should generally precede unnecessary interaction with a digital device at a scene?
options: Document state and follow the preservation procedure
quiz.answer: Document state and follow the preservation procedure
quiz.explanation: Documentation and controlled preservation reduce the risk of changing evidence.

summary: First response emphasizes safety, control, documentation, and preservation.
Live systems require special care.

lessons.title: Acquisition Concepts and Working Copies
lessons.description: Understand logical and physical acquisition concepts, verification, controlled storage, and working copies.
learningObjectives: differentiate logical and physical acquisition concepts

notes.text: Logical acquisition collects selected accessible data; physical or forensic imaging aims to represent storage media at a lower level, subject to device and tool capabilities. The appropriate method depends on the question, authority, device, time, and technical feasibility.

items: Record source, method, date/time, tool or process, destination, and verification values.
Use controlled working copies for routine examination.
Stop and escalate when evidence identity or integrity is uncertain.

practicals.title: Write an acquisition plan
practicals.description: Plan acquisition of a supplied synthetic image without collecting from a live device.
practicals.solution: Keep the plan tool-neutral and lab-safe.
practicals.output: Expected result: a reviewable acquisition worksheet.

quiz.question: Why use a forensic working copy?
options: To examine data while protecting the preserved source
quiz.answer: To examine data while protecting the preserved source
quiz.explanation: Working copies reduce the risk of accidental changes to preserved evidence.

summary: Acquisition is a controlled evidence-representation process.
The method must match the investigative question and be documented.

tasks.title: Create an evidence-preservation runbook
tasks.description: Write a lab-safe runbook for preserving a supplied disk image.
tasks.problemStatement: The runbook must cover intake, hash verification, working-copy handling, access control, notes, and escalation.
requirements: Synthetic disk image or test file
tasks.hint: Use explicit who/what/when/why/how fields for important actions.
tasks.solutionCode:
steps=[
"Confirm case identifier and authority reference.",
"Record source identity and supplied hash if available.",
"Calculate an independent SHA-256 verification hash.",
"Compare and record the result.",
"Create a controlled working copy according to lab procedure.",
"Record working-copy hash and storage location.",
"Restrict access and log transfers.",
"Stop if hashes disagree or evidence identity is ambiguous."
]
for i,s in enumerate(steps,1): print(f"{i}. {s}")
tasks.solutionExplanation: The runbook is deliberately tool-neutral and emphasizes integrity, custody, access control, and stop conditions.

modules.title: Endpoint and Application Evidence
modules.description: Interpret OS, application, filesystem, browser, and communication artifacts with appropriate caution.

lessons.title: Endpoint and Application Artifacts
lessons.description: Interpret operating-system, browser, email, and messaging evidence while distinguishing observations from user intent.

items: OS artifacts may include authentication records, process activity, filesystem metadata, configuration records, and system logs.
Browser and messaging evidence can exist in local databases, caches, downloads, synchronized data, or provider records.
A record of an action is not automatically proof of who intentionally performed it.

notes.text: Artifact paths and formats change with operating-system and application versions. Verify the target version and current documentation in real cases.

practicals.title: Artifact correlation matrix
practicals.description: Correlate synthetic endpoint and application artifacts to one hypothesis.
practicals.output: Expected result: a defensible correlation matrix.

quiz.question: Why correlate independent artifacts?
options: One artifact always proves the case
Correlation can increase confidence and expose contradictions
quiz.answer: Correlation can increase confidence and expose contradictions
quiz.explanation: Independent evidence can corroborate or weaken a hypothesis.

summary: Endpoint evidence is contextual.
Version, provenance, and alternative explanations matter.

lessons.title: Filesystem Metadata and Deleted Data
lessons.description: Interpret filenames, paths, sizes, timestamps, permissions, and deleted-data recovery limits.

notes.text: Metadata can include names, paths, sizes, timestamps, permissions, ownership, and application attributes. Timestamp semantics differ by filesystem, operating system, and application.

items: Preserve original metadata values before normalization.
A timestamp should be interpreted according to its documented event semantics.
Deleted data may remain recoverable if relevant storage has not been overwritten, but recovery is not guaranteed.

practicals.title: Metadata interpretation worksheet
steps: Explain what each timestamp may represent.
State what the metadata cannot establish.
practicals.solution: Use cautious language such as 'indicates' or 'consistent with'.
practicals.output: Expected result: a limitation-aware metadata analysis.

quiz.question: Which statement about a filesystem timestamp is safest?
options: Its meaning depends on the system and event semantics
quiz.answer: Its meaning depends on the system and event semantics
quiz.explanation: Timestamp interpretation requires artifact context and corroboration.

summary: Metadata can support reconstruction but is not automatic proof of intent.
Deleted-data recovery is probabilistic.

tasks.title: Correlate endpoint and communication artifacts
tasks.description: Build a synthetic timeline combining endpoint and communication events.
tasks.problemStatement: Normalize timestamps to UTC, preserve original timestamp strings, sort events, and flag events within five minutes.
tasks.hint: Normalize timezones before comparison and retain original values for traceability.
tasks.solutionExplanation: Temporal proximity is a correlation aid, not proof of causation or attribution.

modules.title: Network and Log Investigation
modules.description: Develop network evidence, log management, normalization, and timeline-analysis skills.

lessons.title: Network Evidence and Attribution Limits
lessons.description: Interpret firewall, DNS, VPN, proxy, flow, and authentication records while understanding IP attribution limitations.
learningObjectives: explain why IP addresses do not directly identify people

items: Network sources may include packet captures, firewall logs, DNS, proxy, VPN, and flow records.
An IP address can represent shared, dynamic, proxied, or compromised infrastructure.
Attribution requires corroboration across identity, endpoint, network, and contextual evidence.

practicals.title: Synthetic network-log analysis
practicals.description: Analyze paired DNS and firewall records.

quiz.question: What is the main attribution limitation of an IP address?
options: It may represent shared, dynamic, proxied, or compromised infrastructure
It always identifies a device owner
quiz.answer: It may represent shared, dynamic, proxied, or compromised infrastructure
quiz.explanation: An address identifies network context, not necessarily a human operator.

summary: Network records provide temporal and communication context.
Attribution requires corroboration.

lessons.title: Log Management and Timeline Normalization
lessons.description: Normalize heterogeneous logs while preserving provenance, timezone assumptions, and gaps.

notes.text: Log management includes generating, transmitting, storing, accessing, and disposing of log data. Investigators must preserve original records and understand retention and clock synchronization.

items: Preserve original timestamp text.
Add source identifiers to normalized events.
Use timezone-aware datetimes.
Do not infer that a missing event proves the event never happened unless logging coverage supports that conclusion.

practicals.title: Normalize synthetic logs
practicals.description: Merge three CSV sources into a UTC timeline.
practicals.output: Expected result: an ordered timeline retaining provenance.

quiz.question: Why preserve the original timestamp in a normalized timeline?
options: It allows traceability back to the source and review of timezone assumptions
It proves the time is correct
quiz.answer: It allows traceability back to the source and review of timezone assumptions
quiz.explanation: Normalization is an analytical transformation and should remain traceable.

summary: Timeline normalization is an analysis step, not replacement of original evidence.
Clock and retention issues affect reliability.

tasks.title: Investigate a synthetic network timeline
tasks.description: Correlate synthetic DNS, firewall, VPN, and endpoint logs.
tasks.problemStatement: Produce a normalized timeline, identify a plausible sequence, document gaps, and separate facts from inferences.
tasks.hint: Validate timestamp parsing and source provenance before interpretation.
tasks.solutionExplanation: Use the timeline to support cautious correlation; do not make person-level attribution from network metadata alone.

modules.title: Mobile, Cloud, and Online Evidence
modules.description: Extend preservation and investigative planning to mobile devices, cloud providers, and public online content.

lessons.title: Mobile Device Evidence
lessons.description: Understand mobile evidence categories, device state, preservation, and acquisition constraints.

items: Potential sources include messages, calls, application data, media, identifiers, location-related records, and authentication artifacts.
Acquisition possibilities depend on device, operating system, lock state, encryption, and authority.
Document device state and examiner interaction before and during approved collection.

notes.text: Do not improvise unlock or bypass procedures on real devices. Use trained personnel and approved methods.

practicals.title: Mobile intake record
practicals.description: Create a synthetic mobile-device evidence record.
steps: Record preservation risks and handoff requirements.
practicals.output: Expected result: a complete intake and preservation record.

quiz.question: What should be documented during mobile evidence collection?
options: Device state, identifiers, condition, and relevant interactions
quiz.answer: Device state, identifiers, condition, and relevant interactions
quiz.explanation: Contemporaneous documentation supports reproducibility and custody.

summary: Mobile acquisition is device- and state-dependent.
Preservation and documentation precede unnecessary interaction.

lessons.title: Cloud and Online Evidence
lessons.description: Plan preservation of provider-held cloud records and public online content with provenance and scope controls.
learningObjectives: explain provider retention and export context

notes.text: Cloud evidence may include authentication records, audit logs, stored objects, messages, configuration records, and provider-generated activity. Public online content may change or disappear after observation.

items: Record provider, account/resource identifiers, date/time, timezone, acquisition method, and export metadata.
Keep source context with received data.
Public-content preservation should capture relevant content and examiner-generated documentation where appropriate.
Provider or cross-border data may require specific legal process.

practicals.title: Cloud/online preservation plan
practicals.description: Draft a synthetic preservation plan for a cloud account and public webpage.
steps: Define investigative questions and date range.
Record source identifiers and time boundaries.
Record legal-process assumptions for later review.
practicals.solution: Keep the request narrow and evidence-linked.
practicals.output: Expected result: a focused preservation/acquisition plan.

quiz.question: Why is provider context important for cloud evidence?
options: Retention, export scope, timestamps, and acquisition context can differ by provider
quiz.answer: Retention, export scope, timestamps, and acquisition context can differ by provider

summary: Cloud and online evidence require source-specific provenance.
Do not assume a downloaded dataset is complete without understanding its export scope.

tasks.title: Design a multi-source preservation plan
tasks.description: Design a preservation plan combining mobile, cloud, and online evidence.
tasks.problemStatement: Address authority, volatility, acquisition context, hashing, custody, storage, and limitations without directing unauthorized access.
tasks.hint: Treat each source as its own evidence stream before defining correlation.
tasks.solutionCode:
plan={
 "mobile":["document state","trained acquisition","custody"],
 "cloud":["define provider scope","record export metadata","hash received data"],
 "online":["record URL/time","preserve content","hash archive"],
 "common":["authority and scope","unique evidence IDs","restricted access","transfer logging"]
}
print(plan)
tasks.solutionExplanation: The plan separates source-specific risks from common evidence controls.

modules.title: Correlation, Attribution, and Reporting
modules.description: Develop hypothesis testing, attribution discipline, anti-forensics awareness, and professional reporting skills.

lessons.title: Hypothesis Testing and Attribution
lessons.description: Test competing explanations and avoid unsupported person-level attribution.

items: State the primary hypothesis.
State plausible alternatives.
List predictions for each.
Map evidence to predictions.
Record contradictions and gaps.
Update the assessment.

notes.text: Attribution is a high-risk inference. Strong conclusions require converging evidence and should explicitly consider alternatives. Anti-forensics indicators can motivate examination but do not identify the actor by themselves.

practicals.title: Competing-hypotheses matrix
steps: Define legitimate-user, compromised-credential, and shared/automated-access hypotheses.
practicals.solution: Do not choose a hypothesis solely because it seems suspicious.
practicals.output: Expected result: a transparent hypothesis matrix.

quiz.question: Which approach is strongest for attribution?
options: Assume the account owner did it
quiz.explanation: Attribution should be based on converging evidence and explicit consideration of alternatives.

summary: Attribution is an inference, not a default property of an artifact.
Anti-forensics indicators require careful interpretation.

lessons.title: Forensic Reporting and Expert Communication
lessons.description: Write findings that are traceable, reproducible, and calibrated to the evidence.

items: Case and authority context
Scope and questions
Evidence inventory and custody
Methods
Findings and supporting evidence
Timeline/correlation
Limitations and alternatives
Conclusion
Appendices and hash records

notes.text: Avoid unsupported claims about intent, identity, causation, or guilt. Use evidence-calibrated language such as 'the records show' or 'consistent with' when appropriate.

practicals.title: Rewrite overconfident findings
practicals.description: Convert unsupported conclusions into evidence-calibrated findings.
steps: Add supporting evidence IDs and limitations.

quiz.question: Which statement is more defensible?
options: The IP proves the suspect committed the crime.
The log records show an authentication from the recorded source at the stated time; the records alone do not establish the person operating that source.
quiz.answer: The log records show an authentication from the recorded source at the stated time; the records alone do not establish the person operating that source.
quiz.explanation: It states the observation and limits attribution.

summary: A forensic report should be reproducible and traceable.
Findings should distinguish evidence from interpretation.

tasks.title: Write a defensible investigation report
tasks.description: Produce a short report from synthetic evidence and event records.
tasks.problemStatement: Include scope, evidence inventory, methods, timeline, findings, limitations, and conclusion. Every finding must cite an evidence identifier.
tasks.hint: Write observations first, then add only the inference supported by the evidence.
tasks.solutionCode:
report={
 "scope":"Synthetic unauthorized-access scenario",
 "evidence":["EV-001","EV-002"],
 "methods":["verified SHA-256","normalized timestamps","correlated authentication and endpoint records"],
 "findings":[{
   "id":"F-001",
   "statement":"Authentication events were recorded from the source shown in EV-001 during the scoped period.",
   "support":["EV-001"],
   "limitation":"The record does not identify the person operating the source."
 }],
 "conclusion":"The documented event sequence is supported within the stated scope; person-level attribution remains unresolved."
}
import json
print(json.dumps(report,indent=2))
tasks.solutionExplanation: The report ties findings to evidence identifiers and avoids unsupported attribution.

modules.title: Final Real-World Project: Synthetic Cybercrime Investigation Casework
modules.description: Complete a realistic but lab-safe end-to-end cybercrime investigation using synthetic records and examiner-created copies.

lessons.title: Project Intake and Evidence Ledger
lessons.description: Prepare the final synthetic case and establish traceable evidence records.
learningObjectives: separate preserved evidence from working products

items: Use unique evidence identifiers.
Record size, SHA-256, receipt time, and notes.
Keep generated reports separate from preserved evidence copies.

practicals.title: Initialize project ledger
practicals.description: Create the project database and add a synthetic file.
steps: Save the supplied code as casework.py.
Run init against a new database.
Run add-evidence with a documented time.
practicals.solution: Use a file created for the course only.
practicals.output: Expected result: a complete evidence row.

quiz.question: What should be established before analysis?
options: Evidence identity, provenance, scope, and integrity
quiz.answer: Evidence identity, provenance, scope, and integrity
quiz.explanation: The project follows an evidence-first workflow.

summary: Intake establishes traceability before interpretation.

lessons.title: Project Timeline and Correlation
lessons.description: Use the pipeline to turn synthetic records into a defensible timeline and findings.

notes.text: The timeline is an analytical model of source records, not the conclusion itself. Students should preserve original values, identify contradictions, and use temporal relationships as clues rather than proof.

practicals.title: Build the project timeline
practicals.description: Import the synthetic events and generate the report.
practicals.solution: Do not modify source data to fit a hypothesis.
practicals.output: Expected result: a traceable timeline and findings.

quiz.question: What is the proper role of temporal proximity?
options: It is a correlation clue requiring other evidence
quiz.answer: It is a correlation clue requiring other evidence
quiz.explanation: Temporal proximity alone cannot establish causation or attribution.

summary: Timeline analysis supports reasoning but does not replace evidence.
Findings must remain traceable.

lessons.title: Final Quality Gate and Case Closure
lessons.description: Audit the final report for technical correctness, traceability, uncertainty, and scope.

items: Confirm scope and authority assumptions.
Confirm every evidence item has an identifier and integrity record.
Confirm timeline provenance.
Confirm every finding has support.
Confirm limitations and alternatives.
Remove unsupported attribution claims.
Confirm no unauthorized collection occurred.

quiz.question: Which condition requires revision before submission?
options: A finding supported by evidence and limitations
A person-level attribution unsupported by the supplied evidence
quiz.answer: A person-level attribution unsupported by the supplied evidence
quiz.explanation: Unsupported attribution is a substantive reporting defect.

summary: Case closure is both technical and analytical review.
A strong report states what is known, how it was established, and what remains uncertain.

project.name: Synthetic Cybercrime Investigation Casework Pipeline
project.description: An end-to-end lab-safe investigation using examiner-created evidence copies and synthetic event records. Students verify evidence integrity, maintain an evidence ledger, normalize timelines, correlate events, and produce a structured investigative report. No live-system acquisition, credential bypass, unauthorized access, or real-target interaction is required.
steps: Create a case workspace containing only synthetic or examiner-created evidence copies.
Record each evidence item with a unique ID, size, SHA-256 digest, receipt time, and notes.
Import synthetic event CSV records and validate timestamps.
Generate a UTC-normalized timeline while preserving original timestamp strings.
Identify clusters, gaps, contradictions, and alternative explanations.
Write at least three findings, each linked to evidence identifiers.
Generate the JSON report and preserve the database and report as working products.
Perform a final quality review of scope, hashes, timeline ordering, finding support, and limitations.
Submit the report with a concise examiner narrative explaining the reasoning.
project.explanation: The project uses Python's standard library to create a local SQLite evidence ledger, hash examiner-created files with SHA-256, import synthetic CSV events, normalize timestamps to UTC, and generate a JSON report. It intentionally does not acquire live systems or alter source evidence. Hashes support integrity checking of compared bytes, not authorship or guilt. Timeline proximity supports correlation but does not prove causation. The report explicitly records limitations and keeps legal conclusions outside the program.
